newsitem.title: USA: Half of Yellowstone buffalo died this winter.
newsitem.headline: Half of Yellowstone buffalo died this winter.

text.p: About half of Yellowstone National Park's buffalo herd has been killed by harsh winter weather or slaughtered to prevent the spread of disease to Montana cattle, the Interior Department said on Friday.
Of the 3,200 to 3,500 buffalo that started the winter, 1,300 to 1,500 remain, the department estimated.
Hundreds have died of starvation or cold, and 1,059 have been shot or sent to slaughter as they wandered in search of food out of the park and onto Montana land, it said.
Ranchers fear the buffalo -- also known as bison -- could spread the disease brucellosis to cattle that will graze on those lands this spring.

"Continued pointless killing by the state of Montana is threatening the future of this magnificent symbol of our nation's commitment to conservation," Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt said in a statement.

"This unacceptable killing of bison must stop. Between the ice and snow and what's left of the harsh winter weather yet to come, and the continued killing by Montana, there is cause for serious concerns of just how many bison will survive," he said.
Babbitt said he will hold a news conference Monday "to review federal proposals to save the last wild, free-roaming bison herd" at Yellowstone.
The massive shaggy buffalo, which was almost exterminated from the Great Plains in the last century, is caught in a conflict among federal agencies and Montana's cattle ranchers.

The Interior Department has sought to maintain the free-ranging herd in Yellowstone, while the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service has threatened to withdraw the brucellosis-free status for Montana's cattle if they share grazing grounds with buffalo.
Brucellosis has little effect on buffalo, but causes cattle to abort calves and produce less milk. There have been no confirmed transmissions of the disease from buffalo to cattle in the wild.
With the threat of losing the disease-free status, Montana ranchers have insisted that the buffalo be destroyed if they cross the park's boundaries.

The Agriculture and Interior departments last month in a letter to Montana Gov. Marc Racicot said if cattle and buffalo mingled, the state would keep its brucellosis-free status if cattle were quarantined and checked for disease.
If the cattle tested disease-free, or if the affected herd were destroyed and no evidence of the disease appeared in neighbouring cattle, the state would keep its status, the departments said.
However, an Interior Department official said about 100 buffalo have been shot on Montana land since that letter.
